verses.translation_literal: And it was after these things: [they] sinned, the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and the baker, against their lord, against the king of Egypt.
verses.translation_dramatic: Some time after these events, a wrong was done inside the palace of Egypt. The king's cupbearer and his baker, the two men who put wine to his lips and bread in his hand, had failed their lord, the king of Egypt.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew is blunt: they 'sinned' (חָטְאוּ), the ordinary word for wrongdoing, not the KJV's mild 'offended', and not the BBE's bureaucratic 'did something against Pharaoh's orders'. In the ancient Near East an offence against the king was an offence against the order of the world, so the word is not too large. Notice the double 'their lord / the king of Egypt': the verse ends by saying the title twice, so we feel how high the stakes are. The text never says what they did. Rashi's tradition has a fly in the cup and a pebble in the loaf, and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan an attempt to poison the king; none of it is in the Hebrew, so the actors must play the fear, not a known crime.

The cupbearer and the baker were not menials but trusted court officers, men who stood closest to the king's mouth and so closest to a poisoner's chance. KJV 'butler' now sounds like a household servant; 'cupbearer' is nearer the rank.

philological_notes.note: The ordinary verb for sin or failing a duty. Here a court offence against the king. It is stronger than KJV 'offended'. The text does not say what the fault was.
One who gives drink; the royal cupbearer. KJV 'butler' (from the keeper of the bottles) is out of date.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh was furious against his two officials, against the chief of the cupbearers and against the chief of the bakers.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Pharaoh's anger broke over his two officers, over the chief of the cupbearers and over the chief of the bakers.
verses.directors_commentary: The anger is named twice with the same word, 'against... against...', and the repeated 'chief of' gives the verse the sound of a sentence being handed down. Radak notes that the text repeats the titles, though the men were just named, to make clear that the anger fell on the chiefs, the ones who had sinned. These are not two servants but the heads of the king's drink and bread, as YLT's 'eunuchs' hints: סָרִיס can mean a castrated courtier, as Ramban notes for palace officers, or simply a high official, as Onkelos took it (compare Potiphar, 37:36). KJV 'officers' and BBE 'servants' are safe but flatten the rank. Pharaoh's rage (קָצַף) is a king's rage; no trial is mentioned, because none was needed.

philological_notes.note: A court official; sometimes literally a eunuch. Ramban gives both readings, saying Onkelos took it as 'princes and great men'. The word is the same as for Potiphar in 37:36.
To be angry, to rage; the anger of one with power to act on it.

verses.translation_literal: And he gave them into [the] custody of [the] house of [the] chief of the slaughterers, into [the] house of the Sohar, [the] place [where] Joseph [was] bound there.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he gave them over to the keeping of the captain of the guard, into his own house, down into the prison, the very place where Joseph already lay in chains.
verses.directors_commentary:
Pharaoh does not send his two ruined officers to a public jail. He hands them to the "chief of the slaughterers", the head of the royal guard, and the guard's own house holds them. The Hebrew title is literally "chief of the butchers"; the KJV's "captain of the guard" is the court rank the word came to carry, and it hides the blunt, bloody noun. BBE's "captain of the army" is further off still.

The prison's name, hasohar, is not in the KJV at all: it simply says "the prison". YLT's "round-house" reflects the usual guess that the word means a rounded or enclosed place, a guess rather than a certainty. Ibn Ezra thought this prison stood inside the captain's own house (Ibn Ezra on Genesis 40:4), which fits the phrasing here, "into the house of the prison" nested within "the house of the chief". Note, too, the last clause, "the place where Joseph was bound there": the narrator reminds us that Joseph is a prisoner already, so the officers arrive as newcomers on his ground. The KJV's "bound" is right; the Hebrew participle ʾasur is the same word that names every prisoner in the chapter.

philological_notes.note: From the root for slaughtering: literally "the slaughterers" or "butchers". As a court title "chief of the slaughterers" means the head of the royal guard, the officers who also carried out executions. English "captain of the guard" keeps the office and loses the noun.

The prison is called the "house of the sohar", a word found almost only in the Joseph story. It is often explained as a round or enclosed place, but that is an etymological proposal, not a settled meaning.
"Bound", "imprisoned". The same passive participle names all three prisoners in the chapter and ties Joseph's fate to theirs.

verses.translation_literal: And the chief of the slaughterers appointed Joseph with them, and he served them; and they were days in custody.
verses.translation_dramatic: The captain of the guard set Joseph over them, and Joseph served them. And so the days passed, one after another, behind the walls.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Appointed' (וַיִּפְקֹד) is an official's word, the one used for assigning an office or a charge; KJV 'charged' and BBE 'put them in Joseph's care' both work. The prisoners have rank and Joseph does not, so this is a slave being put in charge of lords. The verb 'served' (שָׁרַת) is used elsewhere of service in a house or sanctuary, and it is repeated of Joseph again and again in this story; it shows his steadiness.

'Days' (יָמִים) is vague on purpose. Rashi and Rashbam say a full year, and Radak lets it be so, comparing Leviticus 25:29 where the same word means a year. Treat it as 'a long while', not as a number the text gives. KJV 'a season' is nearly right.

philological_notes.note: To appoint, to assign a charge. Rashbam: he put him over all the prisoners' needs.
Days, an unspecified stretch. Rashi and Radak, comparing Leviticus 25:29, take it as up to a year.

verses.translation_literal: And they dreamed a dream, the two of them, each man his dream, in one night, each man according to the interpretation of his dream, the cupbearer and the baker who belonged to the king of Egypt, who were bound in the house of the prison.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then, in a single night, the two of them dreamed. Each man had his own dream, and each dream carried its own meaning, the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, shut away in the prison.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is heavy with repetition: 'dream' appears three times (חֲלוֹם, חֲלֹמוֹ, חֲלֹמוֹ) and 'each man' twice. The sound makes the night feel crowded; two men sleeping a few steps apart, and two dreams arriving together. The phrase 'each man according to the interpretation of his dream' is hard, and the old commentators split. Rashi and Radak: each dream fitted its own meaning. Ibn Ezra: each saw in the dream what would really happen to him. So these are dreams that carry their meaning with them, and not mere nightly noise (Rashbam).

The closing titles repeat that these men 'belong to the king of Egypt' and are 'bound' in the prison. They are the king's men, in a slave's place. Radak points out that they dream in terms of their trades. KJV 'butler' and 'bound in the prison' are accurate; BBE's 'special sense' is a paraphrase.

philological_notes.note: 'According to the interpretation of his dream.' Disputed: each dream matched its meaning (Rashi, Radak), or each man saw in it what would happen to him (Ibn Ezra, Ramban).

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph came in to them in the morning, and he saw them, and behold, they were sullen.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the morning Joseph came in to them. He looked at them, and there they were, dark-faced and silent.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'behold' (וְהִנָּם) puts us behind Joseph's eyes: he sees them and then the narrator makes us see what he sees. זֹעֲפִים is stronger than KJV 'sad' or BBE 'sad': it is the word for a sea in a rage (Ibn Ezra cites Jonah 1:15) and for a sullen, stormy mood (Rashi cites 1 Kings 20). They are dejected, stirred up and angry, not just downcast. Radak says each was troubled because he did not know what his dream meant.

In that world a dream was a message, often from the gods, and an unread message was a threat. Egyptian court dreams were handled by experts, the scribes and magicians (compare Genesis 41:8), and two prisoners had no access to them. So the gloom is practical: no one to read the sign.

philological_notes.note: Sullen, raging, in a stormy mood; the root is used of the sea. Stronger than 'sad'.

verses.translation_literal: And he asked the officials of Pharaoh who were with him in the custody of the house of his lord, saying: Why are your faces evil today?
verses.translation_dramatic: He turned to Pharaoh's officers, who shared his confinement in the house of his master, and asked them gently, "Why do your faces look so dark today?"
verses.directors_commentary:
The sentence is long and slow: 'the officials of Pharaoh who were with him in the custody of the house of his lord.' Ramban says the length is a compliment to Joseph: a young slave puts a question to two great men in the house of the master who hates him, and either could order his head off. Radak and Sforno answer the other way: he could ask because the captain had put the two in his hands, as verse 4 says.

The question itself is short and personal: 'your faces are evil' (רָעִים), literally. KJV 'wherefore look ye so sadly' is a Jacobean flourish; the Hebrew speaks of faces, the place where a man's mood shows. 'His lord' here is the captain of the guard, not Pharaoh. The question is Joseph's kindness at work.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'your faces are evil'; the idiom for a gloomy or troubled look.
'Why', from 'what is known'; a polite request for the reason.

verses.translation_literal: And they said to him, "A dream we have dreamed, and an interpreter there is not of it." And Joseph said to them, "Is it not to God [that] interpretations [belong]? Recount [it], please, to me."
verses.translation_dramatic: "We have dreamed a dream," they said, "and there is no one to read it." The words hung in the dark of the cell. Then Joseph, a slave and a prisoner himself, answered them quietly: "Do not the meanings belong to God? Tell it to me, I beg you."
verses.directors_commentary:
The two officers speak like men with no way out. In Egypt a dream was a letter from the gods, and a dream nobody could read was an unopened letter. Pharaoh's household kept scribes and dream-readers for exactly this, and these two are cut off from all of them. Their complaint is a flat Hebrew clause, "an interpreter there is not of it", with the interpreter placed before the "not" for emphasis. Ramban wonders whether they had already sent to some magicians that morning or asked other men in the prison, and found no one (Ramban on Genesis 40:8; Radak takes the second view).

Joseph's reply is the hinge of the chapter. The KJV's "Do not interpretations belong to God?" is accurate, but it flattens a deliberate move: the Hebrew has the divine name Elohim, and Joseph speaks to Egyptians in the one word they can accept. He does not claim a skill; he claims that meaning is God's to give. Commentators split on what follows. Ibn Ezra holds that only God knows the future, so Joseph's telling cannot help or harm them. Radak reads it as: as God gives dreams, so he gives their meaning. Ramban prefers that God can reveal what is hidden, so "tell me, and perhaps he will show me." The little word na, "please", in "tell it, please", is a courtesy a slave offers to officers who outrank him, and the KJV's old-fashioned "I pray you" carries it only as quaintness.

philological_notes.note: "Interpreter": a participle of the verb "to interpret", used for reading dreams. The noun פִּתְרוֹן, "interpretation", comes from the same root, and the chapter keeps it in view by repeating it (vv. 5, 8, 12, 16, 18).
A plural, "interpretations", with God as the owner. Ibn Ezra observes that the word "interpretation" occurs only with dreams.

A negative question expecting "yes": "Is it not so?" Ramban notes that if Joseph only meant that dreams are God's, the word halo has no force, and so proposes that it works like hinneh, "behold", before settling on his own reading.

verses.translation_literal: And the chief of the cupbearers recounted his dream to Joseph, and he said to him: In my dream, and behold, a vine before me!
verses.translation_dramatic: The chief cupbearer spoke first. He told Joseph his dream: "In my dream, there was a vine before me."
verses.directors_commentary:
The cupbearer opens with a dream-teller's word: 'and behold' (וְהִנֵּה), the sign that we are looking through the dreamer's eyes. In Hebrew he is the 'chief of the cupbearers', so he is not a lowly figure but the head of the king's table; he speaks first because his dream has a gentler face, as the baker's later shows. The word for 'recounted' (סִפֵּר) is the one from verse 8, 'recount it to me': Joseph asks and the cupbearer obeys.

A vine is the right image for a wine-man. Radak (verse 5) says each saw his dream in terms of his own work. Grapes and wine are central to the Egyptian court's life, and the court cupbearer's whole task is to bring the king's cup.

philological_notes.note: 'And behold': the particle that puts the listener inside the dream.

verses.translation_literal: And on the vine, three tendrils; and it was like budding: its blossom went up, its clusters ripened into grapes.
verses.translation_dramatic: On the vine were three branches. It seemed to bud, and in the same breath the blossom rose, and the clusters swelled and ripened into grapes.
verses.directors_commentary:
Everything in this verse happens at once. In the Hebrew the stages follow each other with no gap: budding, blossom, ripe grapes. Ramban reads the kaf of כְפֹרַחַת as 'as soon as' (compare 'as he drew back his hand', 38:29) rather than 'as if' as Rashi had it; the point is speed, and it is what lets Joseph read 'days' in verse 12. Radak agrees: in that very hour the blossom rose and the grapes ripened. Actors should play it as a quickened film, a whole season in one breath.

KJV 'brought forth ripe grapes' is a free paraphrase; the Hebrew says the clusters 'ripened' (הִבְשִׁילוּ) grapes, a verb that is used elsewhere of harvest ripe for the sickle (Joel 4:13, as Ibn Ezra notes). The 'three' is the number that matters. שָׂרִיגִים are long trailing shoots (Rashi), not strong branches.

philological_notes.note: Long trailing shoots or tendrils of a vine (Rashi: long runners); Radak: the vine's boughs.
'As it budded'; the kaf can mean 'as if' (Rashi) or 'as soon as' (Ramban, comparing 38:29). The second makes the speed of events the point.
They ripened; the opposite of unripe fruit (Ibn Ezra), used of harvest in Joel 4:13.

verses.translation_literal: And [the] cup of Pharaoh [was] in my hand, and I took the grapes and squeezed them into [the] cup of Pharaoh, and I gave the cup upon [the] palm of Pharaoh.
verses.translation_dramatic: Pharaoh's cup was in my hand. I took the grapes, and I pressed them into Pharaoh's cup, and I set the cup in Pharaoh's palm.
verses.directors_commentary:
The cupbearer tells it like a man replaying the one act that defined his life. Notice how the verse circles one name: "Pharaoh" comes three times and "cup" three times in a single sentence, so the dream is built from the king and his cup, and nothing in it is the dreamer's own. A cupbearer in Egypt stood closest to the throne and tasted what the king drank; his whole standing rested on that cup. Nothing here is a garden idyll: the vine grows, ripens and is pressed in moments, and the speaker's hands never leave the work.

The unusual verb is "squeezed". Rashi, Rashbam and Radak read it as pressing, as Onkelos does in Aramaic (ʿaṣarit), and Radak cites the Mishnah, "they do not squeeze fruit to extract liquid from it" (Radak on Genesis 40:11, citing Shabbat 147). Ibn Ezra dissents: he compares Isaiah 57:5, "slaughterers of children", and does not accept the Gaon's explanation. The text's verb is the same root as "slaughter", so there is a harsh edge under the harmless act, and the KJV's "pressed" smooths it over. Last, Hebrew says the cup was put "upon the palm" of Pharaoh, and the KJV's "into Pharaoh's hand" loses the picture of the king's open palm.

philological_notes.note: "And I squeezed" or "pressed". The root is the one usually used for slaughter, so English readers lose the echo. Rashi, Rashbam and Radak read it as pressing, as Onkelos does with ʿaṣarit. Ibn Ezra dissents, comparing Isa 57:5 and rejecting the Gaon's reading, as a different view from Rashi and Radak.
"Palm" of the hand. The cup is laid on the open palm of the king, a gesture of service.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph said to him: This is its interpretation: the three tendrils are three days.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Joseph said to him, "This is what it means: the three branches are three days."
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph answers at once and short: no ritual, no pause. The sentence is a pair of threes, 'three... three', and its sound does the work: the tendrils (שָׂרִיגִים) are days (יָמִים). He had said that interpretations belong to God, and now he interprets; the text does not say how he knew, and the commentators ask. Radak: he read the speed of the dream, blossom and ripe grapes in one hour, and so chose days and not months or years. Ibn Ezra offers two more: the king's birthday feast, or the queen's pregnancy.

Ancient Egyptian dream-books worked by wordplay and symbol; Joseph's reading is plain correspondence, three for three. KJV and ASV are exact here. The expansion in Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, with the three branches as the three patriarchs, is a later homily and not in the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: Its interpretation. Ibn Ezra notes the word 'interpretation' is found in Scripture only with dreams.
'Three days': Joseph reads the speed of the dream as the key to its time, days and not months or years.

verses.translation_literal: In yet three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and will restore you to your post, and you will put the cup of Pharaoh in his hand according to the former custom when you were his cupbearer.
verses.translation_dramatic: Three days. Only three more days, and Pharaoh will lift your head from the dust of this place. He will set you back where you stood, and the cup will be in your hands again, passing into his, just as it was in the days before the prison, when you poured his wine.
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph speaks with the calm of a man reporting a forecast, not a hope. The Hebrew 'lift up your head' is an idiom with a double edge, and the reader does not yet know it: here it means 'single you out, call your name', the way a ruler musters a list of servants (Rashi on Genesis 40:13; Rashbam compares Numbers 1:2 'lift up the head of the whole congregation'). Keep the phrase bright and ambiguous; the baker will hear it again in a few verses with the opposite meaning.

The KJV 'restore thee unto thy place' and 'butler' are comfortable English that blurs the job. A משקה was the man who tasted and served the king's drink, a post of intimate trust, because in a palace the cup was the usual weapon. 'Post' translates כן, a stand or base (Rashi: 'your base and your seat'). 'Within three days' in the KJV smooths בעוד שלשת ימים, literally 'in yet three days'. The text then delivers it on 'the third day' (v20).

philological_notes.note: 'Lift up the head' is a deliberate idiom of the whole scene. Here it means to single out or restore; in v19 it means to behead. Rashi and Rashbam read it as 'count, muster' in this verse; Ibn Ezra takes it as a numbering idiom. The English keeps one phrase to preserve the wordplay.
A base or stand, hence a place or office. KJV 'place', ASV 'office'. Rashi glosses it as your base and your seat; Ibn Ezra as your original post.

verses.translation_literal: But if you remember me with you, when it goes well for you, then do, please, loyalty with me, and bring me to remembrance to Pharaoh, and bring me out from this house.
verses.translation_dramatic: But when it goes well with you, when the wine is flowing again, remember me. Do me this kindness, I beg you. Speak my name to Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the only moment in the story where Joseph asks for anything for himself, and the Hebrew is careful, almost formal. The verb pair 'remember' and 'bring to remembrance' (זכר, then the causative הזכיר) turns a private feeling into a public act: first remember me in your heart, then cause Pharaoh to remember me aloud. The cupbearer will fail at the first (v23, 'and he did not remember') and the second, and the same root decides the later scene (41:9).

The KJV 'think on me' keeps only the inward half. 'Kindness' for חסד is also thin: חסד is covenant loyalty, a debt owed to someone who has done you a service. Joseph has just interpreted his dream; he is calling in a favor, politely (נא, 'please'). Note 'this house': the Hebrew has הבית הזה, and in v15 he calls it 'the pit'. The prison belongs to the household of Potiphar's office (40:3), so 'house' is literal.

philological_notes.note: 'Do loyalty with me' is the language of a covenant obligation, not a casual favor. Rashi on נא: it is always a language of request.
Causative of 'remember': 'cause me to be remembered, make mention of me'. Contrasts with the plain זכרתני earlier in the verse.

token_glosses.gloss: and you will bring me to remembrance
and you will bring me out

verses.translation_literal: For I was indeed stolen from the land of the Hebrews, and also here I have done nothing, that they have put me in the pit.
verses.translation_dramatic: I was stolen, truly stolen, from the land of the Hebrews. And here I have done nothing, nothing at all, that they should put me in this pit.
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph's whole biography in one breath, and it is partly a lie of omission. He says 'stolen', not 'sold': the Hebrew passive גנב גנבתי with its emphatic repeated verb ('stolen, I was stolen') drops the brothers entirely, perhaps from protectiveness, perhaps because the Midianite sale (37:28) was in his experience a kidnapping. The KJV 'stolen away' and 'dungeon' both soften. 'Dungeon' for בור hides that this is the same word as the pit his brothers threw him into (37:20-29): the text lets the reader hear that he has been in a hole twice.

'The land of the Hebrews' is an odd phrase in Egyptian ears; 'Hebrew' is the word foreigners use. Radak says he means his father's house in Canaan, Ramban the region where Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived. 'Nothing at all' (מאומה) also corrects the earlier charge: Potiphar's wife accused him of a crime, and Joseph says only that he did nothing, not what was alleged.

philological_notes.note: An emphatic doubling of the passive verb (infinitive absolute plus finite form): 'stolen, I was stolen'. The English repeats the word. It names the brothers' act as theft, not sale.
'The pit', also a cistern; the word used for the pit in 37:20-29. KJV 'dungeon' loses the echo.
'The land of the Hebrews': Radak takes it as the land where the Hebrew patriarchs lived; Ramban gives Hebron and explains the name from Abraham the Hebrew (Gen 14:13).

verses.translation_literal: And the chief of the bakers saw that he had interpreted good, and he said to Joseph, "Also I, in my dream, and behold, three baskets of white bread on my head."
verses.translation_dramatic: The chief of the bakers had been watching, and he saw that the answer was good. So he leaned in toward Joseph. "I too," he said, "I too had a dream. And there, on my head, three baskets of white bread."
verses.directors_commentary:
The baker acts like a man who has waited to see whether the prophet is any good. The text says what he saw: 'he saw that he interpreted good'. Ramban: either he was impressed, or he had been scornful and now dared to speak. Sforno says he hoped Joseph would interpret his dream the same way, since dreams were thought to follow the mouth (Berakhot 55b, cited by Radak). Play him hopeful, not suspicious.

The KJV 'white baskets' is wrong or at least obscure. The Hebrew סלי חרי is disputed: Rashi and Radak take it as baskets of peeled wicker, openwork, from the word for 'hole'; Saadia (cited by Ibn Ezra and Ramban) took it as 'white bread', cognate with Aramaic חור 'white', and Ramban calls that the right reading. The ASV and YLT follow 'white bread'. The Hebrew idiom 'Also I, in my dream' is clipped, as speech of a man who cannot wait: the verb 'was' is missing.

philological_notes.note: Disputed. Either 'baskets of white (bread)' as Saadia is cited by Ibn Ezra and Ramban, or 'openwork baskets' (from חור, hole) as Rashi and Radak. The Jerusalem Talmud (Beitzah 2:6) is cited by Ramban for 'white bread'.
'He interpreted good': the adjective sits before the verb as an adverb. KJV renders it with a noun clause, 'the interpretation was good', and so adds a noun that is not there.

verses.translation_literal: And in the basket, the upper, [was] some of all [kinds of] food of Pharaoh, work of a baker; and the bird [was] eating them from the basket, from upon my head.
verses.translation_dramatic: And in the topmost basket, every kind of food that Pharaoh eats, the work of a baker's hands. And the birds were eating it, out of the basket, from off my head.
verses.directors_commentary:
The baker tells his dream to a man who has just heard good news for his fellow prisoner, so every detail is a plea for the same kind of answer. His basket holds the best a royal baker can make: Pharaoh's own table food, the very trade he practises. The dream has the same props as the butler's, but no act. The butler pressed grapes and put the cup into Pharaoh's hand; the baker carries a basket and watches it be emptied. That contrast is my own reading, not a commentator's.

The KJV's 'bakemeats' is a trap: 'meat' meant food in 1611, and it has nothing to do with meat. 'Uppermost' is fine for the top basket. The KJV also writes 'the birds did eat', but the Hebrew has a participle, 'the bird [is] eating', a scene held in progress, and a singular noun used collectively, as in v19 (הָעוֹף again, 'the bird shall eat your flesh'). That repetition is the point: the same word that fills the dream will fill the verdict. Actors should play the eating as continuous and unresisted. The pronoun 'them' (אֹתָם) is the baked goods, not the birds; the birds are the subject.

The basket stays on his head and the birds eat from it 'from upon my head': close to his skin, helpless, no one drives them off. In a world where an unburied body left to birds was the worst fate, an Egyptian court servant would hear this as an omen long before Joseph speaks.

philological_notes.note: A collective singular, 'the bird(s)', with a singular participle (אֹכֵל), which is why English versions say 'birds'. The same word, in the same singular, returns in v19 where the birds eat the flesh of the hanged man.
'Work of a baker': the finished product of the trade, in apposition to 'food of Pharaoh'. Onkelos renders it עוֹבַד נַחְתּוֹם, 'the work of a baker'.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph answered and said, "This is its interpretation: the three baskets, three days they."
verses.translation_dramatic: Joseph answered, and his voice was level. "This is what it means. The three baskets are three days."
verses.directors_commentary:
The same three days as in the cupbearer's dream: Joseph has the same tool and uses it with the same ease, and that is the cruelty of the scene. The Hebrew is a bare nominal sentence, 'three the baskets, three days they', with no verb 'are' and the pronoun הם placed at the end. Give the line no cushioning. The KJV 'the interpretation thereof' and 'are' are fine but heavier than the Hebrew, which is as short as a verdict.

The baker hears nothing wrong yet: three days is the same number the cupbearer got. Radak reads Joseph's silence on the bread as the clue: the baker's offering never reached Pharaoh, so he would not be restored to his post. The audience should not know the sentence until the next verse.

philological_notes.note: 'Its interpretation': a noun from the same root as the verb for interpreting. Joseph's technical word for solving the dream.

verses.translation_literal: In yet three days Pharaoh will lift up your head from upon you, and will hang you on a tree, and the bird will eat your flesh from upon you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Three days. Only three, and Pharaoh will lift up your head, and it will not be to honor you. He will lift it from your shoulders. Then he will hang you on a tree, and the birds will come, and they will eat your flesh from off you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The same opening as v13, word for word: 'In yet three days Pharaoh will lift up your head.' Joseph does not warn; he lets the phrase turn on itself, adding two words, 'from upon you' (מעליך), which change everything. The KJV 'lift up thy head from off thee' keeps the turn; the BBE 'take you out of prison' and 'give you honour' in v13 loses the paired idiom entirely.

The verb is 'hang' (תלה). In ancient Near Eastern practice, including Egypt and Assyria, the body of an executed criminal could be displayed on a stake or tree; the word does not say whether the man was already dead. Rashbam notes this lifting is not a counting but an actual raising of the head. Radak and the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan read it as beheading first and then hanging. The birds of the dream come true: the baker's body on the tree is the food they eat, and the denial of burial is the worst horror in the law of the text's world. Allow the actor a long silence after 'eat your flesh'.

philological_notes.note: Same idiom as v13, with 'from upon you' added to turn it into beheading. Ibn Ezra: he will remove it from its place or lift it onto a tree. Rashbam: this is the literal lifting of the head, not a counting.
'Hang on a tree' or 'impale on a stake': the Hebrew עץ means tree or wood and does not say how the body was fixed. Targums say beheading first and then hanging.

verses.translation_literal: And it was on the day, the third, the day of the being-born of Pharaoh, and he made a feast for all his servants, and he lifted up the head of the chief of the cupbearers and the head of the chief of the bakers in the midst of his servants.
verses.translation_dramatic: And on the third day, the day Pharaoh had been born, the king made a feast for all his servants. And in the midst of them, he lifted up the head of the chief of the cupbearers, and he lifted up the head of the chief of the bakers.
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph's three days have run out, and the day falls on Pharaoh's birthday: a holiday feast, the one day of the year when a king gives. A royal feast is a moment when a king shows what he does with his power, and Rashi notes that it was called יוֹם גֵּינוּסְיָא, a Greek-derived word for a birthday celebration. Radak allows that the phrase might even mean the day a son was born to Pharaoh, but a yearly birthday is the usual reading.

The verb is the whole drama. Joseph said 'Pharaoh will lift up your head' (נשא) to both men. Here the narrator uses it again, for both men, with no word to say which meaning each gets: restore him, or cut it off. Rashi hears it as a reckoning, 'he counted them', as in the census phrase of Numbers 1. The Hebrew repeats אֶת־רֹאשׁ for each man ('the head of the chief of the cupbearers and the head of the chief of the bakers'); the KJV says only 'the head of the chief butler and of the chief baker', and loses the two separate heads the repetition sets side by side. 'Butler' is a pre-modern word for the keeper of the bottles, so 'cupbearer' is closer to מַשְׁקִים.

The KJV does keep 'among his servants' for בְּתוֹךְ, and that is what matters here. The verdicts are given before the whole court at the feast, not in a prison. Pardon and punishment both become public theatre, and the audience is Pharaoh's own household.

philological_notes.note: A Hophal infinitive, 'being born', with the object marker before Pharaoh. Rashi and Radak both discuss the odd grammar; Radak compares it to Ezekiel 16:4, where the same construction appears.
'Lifted up the head', the same idiom Joseph used for both men. Rashi understands it as 'counted', as in Numbers 1; the sense for each man is only settled in the next verses.

verses.translation_literal: And he restored [obj] the chief of the cupbearers to his cupbearing, and he put the cup on the palm of Pharaoh.
verses.translation_dramatic: The cupbearer was restored to his office. And so it was that he stepped forward, and set the cup into Pharaoh's palm, as if he had never been away.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first half of Joseph's prophecy lands, and it is exact: 'restore' (השיב), 'his cupbearing' (משקהו), and the cup placed in the king's hand. The verse repeats the very words of v13, so the audience hears the promise fulfilled in its own language. The KJV 'butlership' and 'butler' are the old English household title, and the cupbearer was no butler in our sense but a courtier trusted with the king's life. 'Palm' (כף) is the open hand, a literal and more physical image than KJV 'hand'; the cup rests on it.

The verse says nothing of gratitude or of Joseph. The silence is the setup for v23.

philological_notes.note: 'To his cupbearing': the office, not the man. Ibn Ezra distinguishes this noun from the verbal use in v13.

verses.translation_literal: And [obj] the chief of the bakers he hanged, as Joseph had interpreted to them.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the chief of the bakers, him he hanged, exactly as Joseph had told them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The object comes first in the Hebrew: 'And the chief of the bakers, he hanged.' The fronting sets him against the cupbearer of the previous verse in a single stroke, without the narrator adding a word of explanation. The narrator also adds no word of judgment on Pharaoh, and gives no reason for the baker's death; the story treats the king's decision as the weather. The KJV 'But he hanged' adds the contrast word 'but', which the Hebrew gets from word order alone.

The verse ends with Joseph's name and the verb of interpreting, so the reader sees that the whole outcome is credited to his reading, not to Pharaoh's mercy or the men's guilt. 'As Joseph had interpreted to them' is the narrator's confirmation of what was only a claim in vv13 and 19.

philological_notes.note: Object-fronted clause. The word order creates the contrast with v21 where English uses 'but'.

verses.translation_literal: And the chief of the cupbearers did not remember [obj] Joseph, and he forgot him.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the chief of the cupbearers did not remember Joseph. He forgot him. And in the pit, the days went on.
verses.directors_commentary:
The chapter ends on a two-verb sentence: 'did not remember' and 'forgot him'. The verbs are not synonyms stacked for emphasis. Ibn Ezra distinguishes them: 'did not remember' is that he never mentioned Joseph to Pharaoh aloud, 'forgot' is that he put him out of his heart. Rashbam reads 'forgot' as a later, longer lapse. Rashi, citing Psalm 40:5, says Joseph was kept two more years because he trusted a man of Egypt (the 'rahab' of the psalm). Whether Joseph is faulted or only delayed, the narrator offers no comment.

The KJV 'forgat' is archaic English. The sentence also shows what the last scene has done: the root זכר, the thing Joseph begged for in v14, is now negated, and the story's next chapter (41:1, 'at the end of two years') will pick it up. Let the actor drop the line flat; the audience supplies the ache. The ironic twin is the baker, who never forgot anything and was killed; the man who forgot goes on pouring wine.

philological_notes.note: Two verbs, not one repeated. Ibn Ezra: 'did not remember' means he did not mention Joseph to Pharaoh, 'forgot him' means in his heart. Rashbam: the forgetting came later, long after. Rashi gives a moral reading from Ps 40:5.

events.title: Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker offend him
events.narrative_summary: After these things the king of Egypt's cupbearer and baker offend their lord, and Pharaoh is angry with his two officers, the chief of the cupbearers and the chief of the bakers.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'After these things' (40:1) gives no interval. Joseph is already in the prison and in the keeper's trust (39:21–23), so it is anchored 6 months after the start of that stay, with a margin of 6 months; the real interval is unknown. Tier MACRO_ERA since the text gives no count.

events.title: Pharaoh jails the officers and Joseph attends them
events.narrative_summary: Pharaoh puts the two officers in ward in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph is bound. The captain assigns Joseph to serve them, and they remain in custody for some time.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts when the anger ends (40:2–3). 'Days in custody' (40:4): Rashi reads twelve months, Rashbam a full year (as in Lev 25:29), Radak says it is not stated, possibly a year. A 12-month duration is used and the dreams follow it; the figure is the tradition's, not the text's. Tier MACRO_ERA: the text gives only an indefinite 'days' (40:4), no count, so the 12 months are the tradition's estimate and do not raise the tier.

events.title: The cupbearer and baker each dream in one night
events.narrative_summary: Both officers in the prison dream in the same night, each a dream with its own meaning.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'In one night' (40:5), after the days of custody, so anchored on the custody's END at the middle watch (22:00) with 8 hours duration. The margin of 3 months covers how long the 'days' lasted (Rashi's 12 months is one reading). The night, not an hour, is given: DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Joseph sees them dejected and asks why
events.narrative_summary: Joseph comes in to them in the morning and finds them downcast. They say they have dreamed and no one can interpret; Joseph answers that interpretations belong to God and asks them to tell him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'In the morning' (40:6): the first BOKER after the night of the dreams begins, so 06:00 the following day. Short scene of minutes.

events.title: Joseph interprets the cupbearer's dream of the vine
events.narrative_summary: The chief cupbearer tells his dream of a vine with three branches and Pharaoh's cup pressed from its grapes. Joseph says the branches are three days, Pharaoh will restore him, and he asks to be remembered to Pharaoh.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Continuous with the previous scene (40:8 asks him to tell), so it starts when it ends; minutes of speech. No time word of its own: DAY_SEQUENCE for the day of the scene. The three days of 40:12–13 run from this morning.

events.title: Joseph interprets the baker's dream of the baskets
events.narrative_summary: Seeing the good interpretation, the chief baker tells his dream of three baskets on his head and birds eating from the top one. Joseph says the baskets are three days, and Pharaoh will hang him and the birds will eat his flesh.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the cupbearer's interpretation in the same scene ('When the chief baker saw', 40:16), so starts at its end; minutes. DAY_SEQUENCE for the shared day.

events.title: Pharaoh holds his birthday feast for his servants
events.narrative_summary: On the third day, Pharaoh's birthday, he makes a feast for all his servants and lifts up the heads of the two chief officers among them.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'On the third day' (40:20), 'within three days' (40:13, 19). Counting the day of the interpretation as the first, the third day is 2 days after it, as the Gen 22 example counts. Anchored on the END of the baker's interpretation (same morning) with 2 days offset, margin 12 hours for inclusive versus exclusive counting. The feast's duration of 6 hours is a guess, so its tier stays DAY_SEQUENCE.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: On the third day, Pharaoh's birthday

events.title: Pharaoh restores the cupbearer to his office
events.narrative_summary: Pharaoh restores the chief cupbearer to his post, and he puts the cup into Pharaoh's hand.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Inside the feast (40:20–21), anchored on its START with 3 hours offset and 3 hours margin; the order within the feast is not given.

events.title: Pharaoh hangs the chief baker
events.narrative_summary: Pharaoh hangs the chief baker, just as Joseph had interpreted to them.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Inside the feast (40:20, 22), placed a little after the cupbearer's restoration only by the order of the verses; margin 3 hours.

events.title: The cupbearer forgets Joseph
events.narrative_summary: The chief cupbearer does not remember Joseph but forgets him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: From the feast on (40:23). The length is not stated here; 41:1 opens 'at the end of two full years' before Pharaoh's dream, so 2 years is used with the next chapter's session free to refine it. Rashbam: 'a long time afterwards'. MACRO_ERA as a state with no count of its own.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Joseph's word that Pharaoh would hang the baker within three days (40:19) comes true at the feast (40:22).
The chief baker, seeing that the cupbearer's interpretation was good, tells Joseph his own dream (40:16).
Joseph's request to be remembered (40:14) is the favour the cupbearer fails to repay (40:23).
Joseph's word that Pharaoh would lift the cupbearer's head and restore him (40:13) comes true at the birthday feast (40:21).
Pharaoh's anger at the two officers leads him to put them in ward in the prison (40:2–3).
The night's dreams leave the officers dejected, which is what Joseph sees and asks about in the morning (40:5–7).

entities.etymology_meaning: 'Cup of Pharaoh'; the cupbearer's emblem of office.
entities.summary_bio: The king's drinking cup, pressed with grapes in the cupbearer's dream and placed in Pharaoh's hand when the cupbearer is restored.

entities.etymology_meaning: 'His servants' (avadim), the court officials of the king.
entities.summary_bio: The officials and courtiers of Pharaoh's household, guests at his birthday feast, in whose midst he judges the two officers.

entities.etymology_meaning: Title, not a personal name: 'chief of the bakers'.
entities.summary_bio: Pharaoh's chief baker, an unnamed court officer jailed with the cupbearer. Joseph reads his dream of the birds eating from the baskets as his execution in three days, and Pharaoh hangs him on his birthday.

aliases: butler of the king of Egypt
entities.etymology_meaning: Title, not a personal name: 'chief of the cupbearers'; the cupbearer served the king's drink and was a trusted court officer.
entities.summary_bio: Pharaoh's chief cupbearer, an unnamed court officer who offends his lord and is jailed with the chief baker. Joseph interprets his dream of the vine as restoration within three days; restored, he forgets Joseph.

components.evidence_explanation: 40:6: Joseph sees them dejected; it ends only with his hanging in 40:22.
40:3, 40:5: in ward with the cupbearer until Pharaoh hangs him in 40:22.
40:23: the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph but forgot him.
40:6: Joseph sees them dejected; the mood lifts with the good interpretation of 40:12–13.
40:1–2: he is Pharaoh's cupbearer (chief of the cupbearers) when he offends; the office lapses when he is put in ward in 40:3.
40:21: Pharaoh restored him to his butlership, and he gave the cup into Pharaoh's hand; 40:13 calls it 'the former manner'.
40:3, 40:5: put in ward in the prison, 'bound' there, until restored in 40:21.
40:4: the captain of the guard appointed Joseph with them, and he served them.
40:2: Pharaoh was angry against the chief of the cupbearers and the chief of the bakers.

systems.name: Execution by hanging
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Hanging or impalement on a tree or stake was a royal punishment in Egypt and across the Near East, often applied after death and leaving the body exposed to birds.
rules_and_mechanics: The king alone orders the sentence for his officers.
The body is hung on a tree.
Exposure to birds is part of the disgrace.

systems.name: Royal birthday feast
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Royal birthdays or accession days were celebrated in Egypt with banquets for the court; they were also occasions for amnesty and for judgments on officials.
rules_and_mechanics: The king gives a feast for all his servants.
The feast is an occasion on which the king settles the fate of officials in custody.
'Lifting the head' marks either restoration or execution.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Joseph reads the three baskets as three days, after which Pharaoh will hang the baker and birds will eat his flesh.
system_instances.significance_note: The same image of three days has the opposite meaning, showing the dream tracks the dreamer's fate.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Pharaoh hangs the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted.
system_instances.significance_note: Confirms Joseph's gift and gives weight to his later interpretation of Pharaoh's dreams.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Joseph reads the three branches as three days, after which Pharaoh restores the cupbearer to his office.
system_instances.significance_note: Joseph credits interpretation to God and uses the good news to ask the cupbearer to remember him.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Pharaoh puts his cupbearer and baker in ward in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph is held.
system_instances.significance_note: Brings the two officers to Joseph and sets up the dreams that will lead him to Pharaoh.

system_instances.outcome_summary: On the third day Pharaoh holds a feast for his servants and 'lifts the head' of both officers.
system_instances.significance_note: The three-day deadline falls on Pharaoh's birthday, fulfilling both interpretations.

edges.description: The captain of the guard appoints Joseph to attend the two officers.
The restored cupbearer does not remember Joseph and forgets him.
Joseph tells the baker that the three baskets mean death by hanging in three days.
Joseph tells the cupbearer that the three branches mean restoration in three days.
Joseph asks the cupbearer to mention him to Pharaoh and get him out of the prison.
Pharaoh puts the chief baker in ward in the prison.
Pharaoh puts the chief cupbearer in ward in the prison.
Pharaoh restores the chief cupbearer to his office.
